title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired evaluation to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces the incidence of security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators, and a matched sample of N=300 intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline implemented with gpt-5-mini under a frozen protocol (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). The run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300 (shared_initial_candidate semantics). The confirmatory outcome is degenerate: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11=300, n10=n01=n00=0); validators never reported forbidden reachability, so the GVR repair step was never invoked. Paired risk-difference = 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Because the repair path was not exercised, the study does not provide evidence about whether verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations; rather, it quantifies that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline generation already satisfies the safety predicate under the chosen contract. We report the preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, representative validator traces, and a post-hoc upper bound on an undetected baseline violation rate (one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994).

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) offers operational benefits but raises safety concerns: generated configurations can unintentionally change reachability, violate access-control policies, or expand attack surface. Prior work therefore recommends execution oracles and generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops to detect and correct hazardous outputs. The operational efficacy of verifier-in-the-loop designs—specifically their ability to reduce security-increasing misconfigurations under adversarial intents—remains underexplored under preregistered confirmatory designs. We therefore tested this focused question with a preregistered paired experiment. Research question: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? Contributions: (1) a machine-readable preregistration (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) fixing a paired N=300 design and analysis plan; (2) a deterministic Dockerized execution that reuses a single LLM draw per intent pair (shared_initial_candidate) and two deterministic validators; (3) complete execution and analysis artifacts showing a degenerate confirmatory result (baseline and guarded both compliant on all pairs) and explicit discussion of design choices that produced this outcome and how to stress-test GVR pipelines in follow-up work.
sections.related_work: Three strands shaped our design. First, generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures improve correctness for code and infrastructure-as-code tasks but gains vary by verifier strength, task, and model (representative system papers include TerraFormer and related verifier-feedback studies). Second, surveys and NetOps studies document LLM failure modes—hallucination, overconfidence, and domain mismatch—and recommend validators, constrained generation, or human oversight. Third, emulation and testbed work demonstrates feasibility of execution-based validation but cautions about external validity versus production networks. Our experiment sits at the intersection: a preregistered, execution-validated paired test that targets an operational safety predicate (forbidden reachability) rather than purely language-quality metrics. All cited records were verified during the autonomous literature pass and are listed in the bibliography.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The preregistered document (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) specified a paired design with primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability). Sampling: fixed matched sample N=300 (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants; one adversarial variant was generated per benign seed as per the preregistered plan). Intervention and execution contract: for each matched intent we executed (A) baseline: single-pass LLM generation (one LLM call), and (B) guarded: initial LLM generation + verifier check + up to one repair LLM call (GVR). The GVR repair policy (preregistered) issues a single repair prompt only when a validator reports forbidden reachability; at most one repair call is permitted per pair. Generation semantics: shared_initial_candidate — a single initial LLM candidate was generated and re-used for both baseline and guarded playback (this conserved model calls but limits independent-condition variance). Implementation and validators: declared LLM = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json archived). Two deterministic validators were used during scoring: validator_id='deterministic_netops_validator_v5', validator_version='5.0' (these logical identifiers appear in every per-episode validator_trace). The precise validator binaries/configs (Batfish container-image tag/digest, Batfish policy filenames/paths, and the Python static reachability analyzer file SHA-256) are archived in the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) and in the evidence bundle; per the preregistration these artifacts enable full verification of the validator implementations without reproducing exhaustive provenance in the manuscript. Environment, determinism, and scoring: experiments ran inside Docker compositions using FRRouting-style router images; seeds, deterministic sampling parameters, and exclusion rules were preregistered. Per-episode scoring declared a pair 'violating' if any validator reported the forbidden-reachability predicate (logical OR); equivalently, a 'success' required both validators to report no violation. Analysis plan: primary confirmatory test = exact McNemar two-sided paired test (alpha=0.05) on N=300 pairs, with 95% bootstrap percentile CIs computed by resampling (final analysis used 10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed=1729; this increase from the preregistered 1,000 resamples is recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Exclusions and missingness: preregistered exclusion rules and retry policy were followed; deterministic accounting shows zero failed episodes and complete pairs = 300.
sections.results: Execution accounting: planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions), completed episodes = 600, failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 300 under shared_initial_candidate semantics (provider-call audit stage_counts: 'shared_initial_generation' = 300). Primary confirmatory outcome: complete_pair_count = 300; baseline_success_count = 300; guarded_success_count = 300. Paired contingency: n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Repair activity: under the preregistered GVR logic a repair is attempted only when a validator reports forbidden reachability; across the entire run validators never reported forbidden reachability for any initial candidate, so no repair prompts or repair calls were generated (per-episode validator_trace fields show repair_applied=false and repair_prompt_sha256=null in representative traces). Concordance: no verifier disagreement was observed (verifier_disagreement_rate = 0 in the archived per-episode traces). Post-hoc descriptive bound: observing 0 violations in 300 independent episodes yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the underlying baseline violation probability of 1 - 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%); this is explicitly post-hoc and reported as a descriptive bound. Artifact pointers: primary archived artifacts (preregistration and deterministic execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw_results, and analysis outputs) are available in the evidence bundle. For concision we keep provenance metadata in the archived execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) and reference a minimal set of representative artifact hashes in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: the confirmatory result is degenerate because the baseline already satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for every preregistered task under the chosen contract and model. Consequently, the experiment answers whether inserting a verifier changes observed compliance when baseline generation already complies under shared_initial_candidate semantics — and the answer is no — but it does not evaluate whether verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations because the repair path was never exercised. Design choices that explain the null: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics conserved model calls (model_calls_used = 300) but reduced independent-condition variance that could otherwise produce discordant violating outputs; (2) the adversarial-variant generator used here (one programmatic perturbation per benign seed) did not produce verifier-detectable forbidden reachability for the selected model and validators. Practical implications: demonstrating verifier utility requires experimental contracts that exercise the repair path. Recommended protocol changes for future stress-testing experiments: (a) adopt independent-condition generation or increase repair-call budgets so repair paths can be exercised; (b) strengthen adversarial-intent generation via adversaries specifically targeting verifier predicates; (c) evaluate multiple LLM families and stronger oracles; (d) include device heterogeneity and live-traffic conditions to improve external validity. Threats to validity: internal validity concerns include prompt sensitivity and the shared-generation contract; construct validity questions whether the chosen forbidden-reachability predicate and the two deterministic validators capture operational security risk; external validity is limited by the synthetic task bank, single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini), and Dockerized emulation. The archived preregistration and execution manifest document these threats in detail.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation using gpt-5-mini over 300 matched intents. The confirmatory outcome was degenerate: both baseline and guarded conditions passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11=300). Because validators never reported violations, the repair path was not invoked and the study cannot determine whether GVR repairs would rescue genuine violations. This null highlights that experimental-contract choices—generation semantics (shared vs independent), adversarial potency, repair budget, verifier strength, and model diversity—materially determine whether verifier-in-the-loop architectures can demonstrate benefits in NetOps security. Future work should intentionally design experiments that exercise the repair path (independent draws, stronger adversaries, multi-model comparisons, and richer oracles). A descriptive post-hoc bound indicates an upper 95% limit on an undetected baseline violation rate of ≈0.00994 (one-sided Clopper–Pearson), but this does not substitute for experiments that invoke repairs. All preregistered artifacts, per-episode traces, and analysis outputs are archived to enable verification and to guide follow-up stress-testing designs.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11=300, n10=n01=n00=0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; the execution/task_manifest.jsonl archived in the evidence bundle contains per-task generation_seed and task_payload (intent text and difficulty annotations). If readers require the exact adversarial-transformation code or step-by-step transformation logs, those artifacts are archived in execution/execution_manifest.json (refer to the manifest for the precise transformation artifact identifiers).

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.

Provenance in archive: precise container-image tags/digests and validator file SHA-256 values are preserved in the archived execution manifest rather than printed exhaustively inline to preserve manuscript concision; consult execution/execution_manifest.json in the evidence bundle for those exact identifiers.
